metadata.title: Claude, On Message
metadata.subtitle: The Marketing Plugin
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: what does the marketing plugin actually change about working with Claude? Take the plugin apart, explain how each of the five capabilities works, name the design choices, and land the carry-out that it turns Claude into a collaborator that plans, watches competitors, and reads your numbers with you — but only gets specific once you do, and the judgment stays yours.

beats.narration_text: Liam here, in for Bear. Here's what actually happens when you install the marketing plugin: it isn't a faster content generator. It plans, analyzes, and refines — because they optimized for judgment, not throughput. So what does that actually change?

props.text:
The marketing plugin
is just a faster way

What does it actually change?

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. If you run a business, you already run marketing — whether or not you'd call yourself a marketer. Content, campaigns, competitor tracking. And in the middle sits the decision nobody else can make for you: what to say, to whom, and where.

production_viz.label: YOU'RE ALREADY DOING MARKETING
production_viz.caption: what to say, to whom, where

beats.narration_text: Most marketing tools stop at 'write me a blog post.' That's a design choice — they optimized for output volume and punted on strategy. This plugin plans, analyzes, and refines. The trade-off: a slower interaction that produces something closer to a plan than a paragraph. The alternative is the brief scrawled between meetings, half a thought handed to whoever's free. That math changes when the collaborator already knows your brand.

production_viz.label: MORE THAN A DRAFTING TOOL
production_viz.caption: a collaborator, not a vending machine

beats.narration_text: Here's the machinery. Five capabilities under one install: creating content, planning campaigns, reading competitors, interpreting performance, and holding your brand consistent. They chose one shared context over five separate apps — the price is that everything happens in text; the gain is that context carries between tasks without a hand-off.

Content creation isn't a single-shot 'write me a post.' It's a pipeline — brief, outline, draft, variations — each stage a distinct call the model can revisit. Email sequences, social calendars, landing-page copy, ad variants, all shaped by the voice and audience you configured once.

production_viz.label: CONTENT CREATION
production_viz.caption: shaped by your voice and audience

beats.narration_text: Campaign planning runs the same pipeline, wider. Tell it what you're launching, who you're reaching, what you want them to do. It builds a messaging framework, picks channels, and lays out execution. The design bet: put the strategic decisions in the same tool that will draft the outputs, so the frame and the copy don't drift apart.

Competitor reads run through the same collaborator. How rivals position themselves, who they're aimed at, what they claim. Then the interesting move: it looks for the gap — the angle nobody's working, the audience nobody's talking to. This is design-lens work, not spec-sheet work — it evaluates the space around the competitors, not just the competitors themselves.

Connect your analytics and it reads the campaign data with you. This is the interesting one. Most tools stop at 'here are the numbers.' This one goes to 'here's what the numbers suggest you do next.' They chose interpretation over dashboard — you get a smaller amount of information that means more.

And it holds the brand line. Configure voice, tone, terminology once, and it enforces them across every output — which matters most at volume, the exact moment consistency slips in a human team. The trade-off: you have to write the config carefully; the plugin isn't guessing your brand, it's applying what you handed it.

Out of the box, it works. But out of the box is the vending-machine version. The real gain hides in customization — and customization is three inputs: your brand voice, your audience, and what you actually sell. That's it. Three fields, filled once.

shot.new_visual_element: THE SETUP THAT PAYS FOR ITSELF

production_viz.label: THE SETUP THAT PAYS FOR ITSELF
production_viz.caption: three inputs, once

beats.narration_text: Specificity is the lever, and this is where most people leave the value on the table. 'Professionals' is nearly useless — it names a category too big to aim at. 'Small-business owners considering AI tools but not technical' — that's something the model can actually work against. The narrower the target, the sharper everything downstream, because the model has fewer priors to average across.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — SPECIFICITY IS THE LEVER

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — SPECIFICITY IS THE LEVER
production_viz.caption: the narrower, the sharper

beats.narration_text: Voice is calibrated by example, not description — and that's a design choice that matters. The model is much better at imitating text than at obeying adjective lists like 'professional but friendly.' Show it a few paragraphs you've actually written, tell it who you're reaching, and it calibrates to those examples — not to a generic house style.

Fifteen minutes of this changes the output measurably. Content comes back closer to your voice. Ideas ground in your actual business instead of a generic version of it. Competitive analysis narrows to the players who actually matter. Here's why the number moves so much: eighty-percent-right on the first draft is a completely different edit from fifty-percent-right. The first is polishing; the second is rewriting.

Instead of staring at a blank month, say: build me a calendar — two posts a week, a weekly newsletter, two blog pieces, for this audience, on these themes. It returns a structured calendar with a specific idea in every slot. The design shift is small but load-bearing: you're editing a plan, not inventing one. That's a completely different cognitive task.

production_viz.label: THE CONTENT CALENDAR
production_viz.caption: editing a plan, not inventing one

beats.narration_text: Say you're launching a new service next month. Ask for a five-email sequence aimed at subscribers who know you but have never bought — it drafts the whole arc: subject lines, body copy, calls to action, each email building on the one before. You add the personal anecdotes it can't know — the plugin doesn't fake those, which is the right choice — and the sequence is ready to load.

production_viz.label: THE EMAIL SEQUENCE
production_viz.caption: each email builds on the last

beats.narration_text: Repurposing is the tedious work everyone skips because it feels like a chore, not a skill. One long blog post becomes five social posts, a newsletter intro, and a short video script — from a single source, in one pass. This is where the plugin saves real hours, and it's the least glamorous answer to 'what did it change.'

And the monthly reckoning: which pieces landed, which fell flat, is there a pattern? Feed it your metrics and it goes past the numbers to what they mean for next month. Across all five workflows the shift is the same — you're editing a plan, not staring at a blank page. That's the single mechanism the whole plugin is optimizing for.

Four habits separate the people who get value from the people who get slop. Frontload the brand configuration. Ask for variations, not one answer. Delegate the formats you dread — captions, subject lines, meta descriptions, the stuff nobody enjoys — and delegate them specifically. Review everything. That last habit is doing more work than it looks like it's doing.

Ask for options, not answers. 'Give me five angles on this headline' beats 'write me a headline' almost every time. Here's why: the spread of five is showing you the model's map of the space. One guess hides the map. Choosing from options is faster and better than debating a single output.

But review everything that goes public. The plugin drafts well; your touch is what makes it yours. It won't replace your CMO — that's not what it was optimized for. What it does replace is the moment you start every draft from a brief scrawled between meetings. You keep the judgment; it takes the grind. This works if you value judgment; it fails if you were hoping to skip that step.

So here's the carry-out. The marketing plugin turns Claude from a content generator into a collaborator that plans, watches competitors, and reads your numbers with you. But it only gets specific once you do. And the judgment stays yours — by design, not by accident.

props.quote: The marketing plugin turns Claude from a content generator into a collaborator — it plans, watches competitors, and reads your numbers with you. But it only gets specific once you do, and the judgment stays yours.

beats.narration_text: Here's a prompt you can paste right now into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — no marketing plugin required — that runs the fifteen-minute brand interview this whole video is about. It hands you back a short config you can reuse everywhere. Go deeper: what campaign would be a bad first fit for you, and what does that tell you about your actual strengths?

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to configure a marketing collaborator I can trust — an AI I'll ask to plan campaigns, read competitors, and interpret my performance data. Here's what you know about me: [paste two or three paragraphs you've written in your own voice, and one sentence on what you sell]. First, describe my voice back to me in five to eight adjectives, with two examples of moves I make that most writers don't. Second, ask me three specific questions that would let you name my target audience more sharply than 'professionals' or 'small businesses.' Third, once I answer, hand me a short brand config — voice, audience, positioning — that I can paste into any AI tool going forward. Then name the single first campaign we should build together, and why that one.
